newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French insurer resists govt call to quit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French insurer resists govt call to quit.

text.p: The chairman of French state-owned insurer GAN is refusing to quit after a government call for his resignation in the wake of a failed attempt to privatise his group's banking subsidiary, Credit Industriel et Commercial.

The next step would be a decree to fire Jean-Jacques Bonnaud, whose head is on the block along with that of CIC chairman Bernard Yoncourt after the government decided last week to abandon a CIC sell-off tender which drew just one eligible offer, from Banque Nationale de Paris.

"He is not resigning," said a GAN spokeswoman on Tuesday. Bonnaud was due to meet Finance Minister Jean Arthuis when the latter gets back at the end of the week from a trip to Japan with President Jacques Chirac.

The decision to demand Bonnaud's departure was announced by the finance ministry on Monday in agreement with Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who crossed swords with Bonnaud in February over an attempt by Juppe to place a close advisor at the head of CIC.

Juppe backed down after his attempt to place Pierre-Mathieu Duhamel sparked a storm of controversy over the government's role in appointments at state companies, after which Bonnaud named Yoncourt head of Credit Industriel et Commercial (CIC).
Yoncourt infuriated Arthuis in October after declaring on television, in the middle of the privatisation tender process, that a sale to a major French bank could spell "death" for CIC.
CIC is a group of 11 regional banks whose main forte is its strong local position and relations with a clientele of large and medium sized corporates.
Arthuis reacted harshly to Yoncourt's remarks at the time, describing them as unacceptable and threatening to "draw the consequences".
The irritation showed through again last week when Arthuis announced the scrapping of the sell-off tender and broke from his usually guarded rhetoric to criticise Bonnaud and Yoncourt.
"The managers of GAN and CIC did not behave in a way to encourage progress in this process," he said at the time.
The government received only two bids for CIC -- from BNP and Societe Generale.

The French privatisation commission rejected the offer from Societe Generale on the grounds it did not comply with the terms imposed by the government, of which the most important is that any buyer must preserve the bank's regional integrity.
Arthuis said he was determined to privatise the group but that he was breaking off a tender in which there was only one eligible offer on the table to take more time to reflect.
Staff and trade unions opposed the sell-off with strikes and protests over feared job losses but the spectre of a break-up of the group also sparked widespread fears among local politicians.
Banking analysts say the strict government conditions on the sale could only attract a low-price offer for CIC, which is valued at around 14 billion francs ($2.75 billion) on GAN's books.
That would correspond to about 9.4 billion francs for the 67 percent which the government had put up for sale.
The CIC privatisation had been seen as a prerequisite to selling off GAN, or Groupe des Assurances Nationales, itself.
